scenes.heading: Channels
scenes.narration: Let's look at channels, Go's typed conduits that let goroutines communicate safely by passing values instead of sharing memory.

scenes.heading: The core idea
items: Unbuffered channels synchronize sender and receiver
scenes.narration: A channel is a typed pipe: the arrow operator sends a value in one direction and receives it in the other. On an unbuffered channel a send blocks until a receiver is ready, so the two goroutines rendezvous at that instant. This is Go's motto in action — don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.

scenes.heading: Anatomy of an unbuffered send
steps: A goroutine runs `ch <- v` and parks
The value is copied directly across
Both send and receive complete together
scenes.narration: When a goroutine sends on an unbuffered channel with no waiting receiver, it parks in the channel's send queue. When another goroutine receives, the runtime hands the value directly across, and both operations complete at the same instant. Because the send finishes only when the receive does, this establishes a happens-before relationship — the sender's earlier writes are guaranteed visible to the receiver.

scenes.heading: Producer, close, and range
scenes.narration: Here a producer goroutine sends the values one through four and then closes the channel. The consumer uses for-range, which receives values until the channel is closed and drained, then ends the loop. Notice the producer is the one that closes the channel — that is the rule. Forgetting to close it would deadlock the range loop, since it would wait forever for a fifth value.

scenes.text: Only the sender closes, exactly once. Sending on a closed channel panics; receiving returns the zero value, ok == false.
scenes.narration: Closing has strict rules. Only the sender should close a channel, and only once. Sending on a closed channel panics, while receiving from one never panics — it returns the element's zero value with ok set to false, which is how the comma-ok receive detects a closed channel.

scenes.text: Make ownership explicit: who sends, who closes, and how every goroutine exits.
scenes.narration: The discipline that makes channel code safe is clear ownership. Decide who sends, who closes, and how every blocking goroutine exits, and channels become a clean, race-free way to build pipelines and worker pools.
